newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: S.Korean, Japanese car makers prepare Europe assault.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean, Japanese car makers prepare Europe assault.

text.p: While European car makers complain about overcapacity, tiny profit margins and political interference, Japanese and South Korean manufacturers are preparing for a major assault on the continent's motor market.

Typifying the problems of the European car industry, France's Renault SA has created a political storm with plans for dismissing workers en masse to tackle heavy losses and to prepare for deregulation of the market in the year 2000.
But the Asians are undaunted by the tough conditions.

South Korean car makers have established a bridgehead in Europe and are preparing the next stage of their campaign while the Japanese, recovering from strong yen bruising, will be tough contenders again soon.
South Korean car makers, mainly Daewoo Motor Co and Hyundai Motor, have now achieved a market share of just under two percent, up from almost nothing five years ago.
The Japanese, after peaking at around 12.3 percent in 1991, have slipped to just over 10.5 percent, hammered back by the strength of the yen.
But the big European car makers will have to watch out. Ford of Europe chairman Jacques Nasser said on Tuesday at the Geneva car show that South Korean and Japanese sales were a big threat to jobs.
Experts say that as European car sales stagnate, increasing competition from the east will make it very difficult for European car makers to hold on to market share.

Toyota Motor Corp, Nissan Motor Co Ltd and Honda Motor Co Ltd are all producing cars in Europe in a big way, mainly in Britain. They made 715,000 in all of Europe last year, with output forecast to rise to 1.2 million by 2000, according to the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) of London.
The weaker yen now offers more profitable exports from Japan, and with the opening of European markets in 2000 to unlimited car imports, the Japanese are building up into a major threat again.

"The Japanese threat has diminished over the last few years. But they are clearly on the rebound, and when formal constraints are removed after 2000, watch out for the Japanese," said Ian Robertson, director of the EIU's automotive group.
Robertson said that after 2000, when sales were not controlled, Japanese car makers would be able to offer a much more varied lineup of cars.
The EIU expects Japanese market share to reach 12.3 percent in 2000. South Korean penetration should reach 3.5 percent.
J.D.Power-LMC Automotive Forecasting expects Japanese share to reach 11-12 percent by 2000, but says this is a conservative estimate. The South Koreans could reach three percent.
Some analysts say it is relatively easy to get two percent of the market, but it will be much more difficult expanding from there.

"That's what they said about the Japanese. The Koreans have studied what the Japanese did, they've looked at the mistakes," said Peter Cooke, director of the Henley Centre's automotive management group. "They won't necessarily stay at the bottom end of the market."
Some analysts say South Korean companies are using their financial muscle to underpin their low prices in Europe but they are not without problems.
"There are some warning signs," says the EIU's Robertson.

"Daewoo in the U.K. has been shipping out used cars back to Korea to shore up residual (second-hand) values. They've been making a loss on their world-wide vehicle operations.... and are having to face some of the consequences of their very fast global investment strategy," Robertson said.

EIU consultant Colin Whitbread said the Japanese companies would be even more formidable after surviving the traumas of the strong yen. "The financial strength of the Japanese is improving every day. They went back to the drawing board to produce cars that made money with the yen at 80 to 90 to the dollar, now it's around 120," said Whitbread.

"They can be a lot more competitive; that would squeeze inefficient producers in Europe. What will they choose to do -- sit back and make more money from the higher margins, or go out and attack markets for higher market share?" Whitbread said.
John Lawson, automotive analyst at investment bank Salomon Brothers is more sanguine.

"The Europeans have lived with competition for a long time. I'm not convinced that the Japanese currently provide a major new threat. They are recovering some of their poise, but they are not gaining much ground and I'm not expecting them to gain back all that much," Lawson said.
